ABSTRACT
Objective: Maxillary sinus mucosal cysts represent prevalent oral and maxillofacial diseases, and their precise diagnosis is 
essential for surgical planning in maxillary sinus floor elevation. This study aimed to develop a deep learning-­based pipeline for 
the classification of maxillary sinus lesions in cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) images to provide auxiliary support for 
clinical diagnosis.
Methods: This study utilized 45 136 maxillary sinus images from CBCT scans of 541 patients. A cascade network was designed, 
comprising a semi-­supervised maxillary sinus area object detection module and a maxillary sinus lesions classification module. 
The object detection module employed a semi-­supervised pseudo-­labelling training strategy to expand the maxillary sinus an-
notation dataset. In the classification module, the performance of Convolutional Neural Network and Transformer architectures 
was compared for maxillary sinus mucosal lesion classification. The object detection and classification modules were evaluated 
using metrics including Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1 score, and Average Precision, with the object detection module addition-
ally assessed using Precision-­Recall Curve.
Results: The fully supervised pseudo-­label generation model achieved an average accuracy of 0.9433, while the semi-­supervised 
maxillary sinus detection model attained 0.9403. ResNet-­50 outperformed in classification, with accuracies of 0.9836 (sagittal) 
and 0.9797 (coronal). Grad-­CAM visualization confirmed accurate focus on clinically relevant lesion features.
Conclusion: The proposed pipeline achieves high-­precision detection and classification of maxillary sinus mucosal lesions, 
reducing manual annotation while maintaining accuracy.
1   |   Introduction
Bone volume insufficiency in the posterior maxilla presents a 
prevalent challenge in implantology [1]. To address this issue, 
maxillary sinus floor elevation is commonly undertaken, a 
procedure wherein the maxillary sinus mucosa is separated 
from the bone wall, and bone substitute material is introduced 
to achieve adequate bone volume for implant placement [2]. 
However, the maxillary sinus mucosal lesions, particularly 
mucosal cysts, constitute the primary risk factor for proce-
dural failure [3]. Maxillary sinus mucosal cysts (MSCs) exhibit 
a high prevalence, with population detection rates up to 35.6%

[4]. The currently widely adopted classification system stems 
from the research of oral pathologist Gardner in 1984, who 
categorized these lesions into three distinct types: pseudo-
cysts, retention cysts, and mucoceles [5].
The presence of MSCs poses a significant challenge in max-
illary sinus floor elevation procedures [6]. Clinical manage-
ment strategies for MSCs encompass direct surgery with cyst 
retention, surgery following cyst content aspiration, and ei-
ther staged or simultaneous bone augmentation after cyst re-
moval [7]. The type, dimensions and location of cyst directly 
influence both the surgical approach and prognosis [3, 8–11]. 
Pseudocysts, typically containing serous fluid, are amenable 
to puncture and decompression [12]. In contrast, retention 
cysts, filled with viscous secretions, may lead to maxillary 
sinus mucosal perforation, thereby increasing the complex-
ity of simultaneous surgical intervention [13]. While direct 
surgery with cyst retention simplifies the surgical procedure, 
it may elevate the risk of postoperative maxillary sinusitis, 
potentially due to cystic obstruction of the maxillary ostium 
[14]. Accurate diagnosis of maxillary sinus mucosal lesions on 
CBCT images necessitates specialized radiological expertise 
and extensive clinical experience, posing a considerable chal-
lenge for junior dentist. Even experienced specialists may face 
an increased risk of misdiagnosis due to cognitive fatigue in 
high-­intensity clinical environments.
In recent years, deep learning techniques have demonstrated 
remarkable efficacy in medical image analysis. Convolutional 
Neural Networks (CNNs) and Transformers represent the two 
most prevalent architectures in this field. CNNs achieve feature 
extraction through local receptive fields and weight sharing, while 
Transformers employ self-­attention mechanisms to model long-­
range dependencies [15, 16]. In the oral domain, various CNNs 
models have been successfully applied to tasks such as caries 
detection, gingivitis classification, implant stability evaluation 
and surgical guide design [17–21]. Concurrently, Transformers, 
as a novel generation of deep learning architecture, are being ex-
plored in diverse medical image processing tasks, leveraging their 
robust global modeling capabilities. Transformers have been im-
plemented in medical image classification, segmentation, object 
detection, and other tasks, often surpassing the performance of tra-
ditional CNNs [22–24]. However, the application of Transformers 
in dentomaxillofacial radiology remains in its nascent stages, with 
their potential in CBCT image analysis yet to be fully explored.
Previous investigations have initiated preliminary explorations 
into the application of deep learning techniques for maxillary 
sinus lesions diagnosis. Researchers have proposed deep learning 
models based on diverse algorithms to achieve automatic segmen-
tation of the maxillary sinus in CBCT and panoramic radiography 
[25–29]. Subsequently, researchers developed intelligent diagnos-
tic decision-­making schemes for maxillary sinus lesions. Zeng 
et al. developed a maxillary sinus abnormality screening model 
integrating YOLOv5 and ResNet-­50 algorithms, which combines 
the diagnostic functions of maxillary sinus localization and ab-
normality classification [30]. Ha et al. constructed an AI model 
utilizing the EfficientDet-­D4 algorithm for classification of max-
illary sinus conditions on panoramic radiographs (categorized as 
healthy, pseudocyst, tumor or cyst) [31]. Kuwana et al. employed 
the DetectNet object detection algorithm to achieve automatic 
detection of the maxillary sinus on panoramic radiographs and 
completed the classification and diagnosis of maxillary sinus sta-
tus (categorized as healthy, inflammation, or cysts) using an object 
detection approach [32]. Additionally, other researchers have de-
veloped AI models for tasks such as maxillary sinus lesion region 
segmentation and inflammation grading [33–35].
Existing studies predominantly focus on the detection and clas-
sification of maxillary sinus abnormalities as a whole, while in-
telligent diagnostic models specifically targeting MSCs remain 
relatively scarce. This study proposes a cascade network archi-
tecture specifically designed for the detection and classification 
of MSCs in CBCT images. Semi-­supervised learning can exploit 
latent features from unlabeled samples to enhance training effi-
cacy [36]. We employ a semi-­supervised pseudo-­labeling strategy 
to annotate the maxillary sinus dataset using a model trained on 
a small-­scale labeled dataset. This approach aims to mitigate the 
burden of manual annotation while augmenting the size of the 
maxillary sinus detection dataset. Furthermore, we systematically 
compare the relative merits of CNNs and Transformer architec-
tures for maxillary sinus image classification. Ultimately, the clas-
sification results of maxillary sinus lesions outputted from this 
cascade network can serve as a diagnostic aid for clinicians.
The primary contributions of this study are as follows:
1.	 Implementation of semi-­supervised learning techniques 
for generating pseudo-­labels to expand the small-­scale 
maxillary sinus detection dataset, thereby increasing the 
size of sagittal and coronal plane object detection datasets 
while simultaneously reducing the annotation workload.
2.	 Comprehensive comparison of CNN and Transformer ar-
chitectures in the maxillary sinus image classification task 
across multiple dimensions, identifying the most suitable 
model for this specific application. The resultant classifi-
cation outputs will assist in clinical diagnosis and help de-
velop appropriate treatment plans.
2   |   Materials and Methods
2.1   |   Ethical Standards
This study adhered to the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki 
(revised 2000) and was approved by the Ethics Committee of the 
Stomatological Hospital of Guangzhou Medical University (No. 
LCYJ2023005). The research protocol complied with the Checklist 
for Artificial Intelligence in Dental Research guidelines [37], and 
the TRIPOD guidelines for prediction model development and 
validation. All participants provided written informed consent. 
Personal identifiers were removed through comprehensive ano-
nymization to safeguard privacy and confidentiality of participant.
2.2   |   Patients Collection
This retrospective study encompassed 541 patients who 
sought treatment at the Department of Oral Implantology, 
Affiliated Stomatological Hospital of Guangzhou Medical 
University, between March 15, 2018 and June 30, 2022. The

Exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) Age below 18 years; (2) 
History of maxillary sinus surgery; (3) CBCT images exhibit-

2.3   |   Radiographic Diagnosis of Maxillary Sinus 
Lesions
Three oral radiologists, each with 5 years of experience, eval-
uated bilateral maxillary sinus CBCT images for each patient. 
The maxillary sinus conditions were classified into the follow-
ing categories: pseudocysts, mucocele, mucosal thickening, 
retention cyst and normal. The radiological diagnostic crite-
ria are shown in Table S2, and Figure S1 shows some related 
image examples. The Fleiss' Kappa analysis of 50 randomly 
selected CBCT images showed excellent inter-­examiner reli-
ability (κ = 0.82, p < 0.001).
2.4   |   Data Set Construction
The study comprised 541 patients (mean age: 43.9 ± 2.8 years; 
♂:♀ = 1.19:1), with 232 cases from CBCT 1 and 309 cases from 
CBCT 2. Among all cases, 85 (15.71%) were diagnosed as pseudo-
cysts, 118 (21.81%) as retention cysts, 30 (5.55%) as mucocele, 
and 308 (56.93%) as mucosal thickening.
According to standardized image acquisition pipeline 
(Figure  S2), CBCT data were imported into CS 3D Imaging 
Software (version 3.4.3, Carestream Dental LLC, Atlanta, GA, 
USA) for sagittal and coronal slices. With a slice thickness 
of 0.3 mm and slice interval of 1 mm, this process generated 
35 165 sagittal slices and 25 968 coronal slices. The maxillary 
sinus area annotation process was conducted by an oral radiol-
ogist (Xueqi Guo) using LabelMe (version 5.0.1, Massachusetts 
Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA, USA). Subsequently, 
a labeled dataset was constructed by randomly selecting 800 
slice images from each of sagittal and coronal planes (1600 
in total) for training the pseudo-­label generation model. The 
trained model was then employed to automatically label the 
remaining 59 533 unlabeled slices. Images with confidence 
scores above 0.7 from the automatically labeled dataset, along 
with manually labeled data, were utilized to train the maxil-
lary sinus detection model.
The maxillary sinus detection model was applied to all 61 133 
sagittal and coronal images, resulting in 45 136 maxillary sinus 
images identified as regions of interest (ROI). Based on the 
radiologists' diagnoses of each patient's CBCT, 4321 images 
with distinct lesion characteristics were extracted from the de-
tected maxillary sinus images. To mitigate class imbalance in 
the dataset, 20% of the normal maxillary sinus images (8163 
images) were randomly selected as part of the model devel-
opment dataset. Finally, the selected maxillary sinus images 
were divided into two subsets according to sagittal and coronal 
orientations for subsequent classification model training and 
testing (Figure 1A).
2.5   |   Construction of Cascade Network
The proposed cascaded network architecture comprises two 
principal modules (Figure 1B,C). The first is a semi-­supervised 
maxillary sinus area object detection module, which utilizes 
Tiny-­YOLOv4 as its network and implements a semi-­supervised 
learning strategy to construct a maxillary sinus detection model. 
This module's workflow involves initially training the model 
with a limited set of labeled samples, followed by the genera-
tion of pseudo-­labels for a substantial corpus of unlabeled data. 
Subsequently, semi-­supervised training is executed on the amal-
gamated dataset of both genuine and pseudo-­labeled instances, 
culminating in the development of a robust maxillary sinus 
detection model. The output of the maxillary sinus detection 
model is cropped to obtain the ROI, which serves as the input 
for the subsequent classification module.
The second module is a classification and diagnosis component 
based on the ResNet-­50 architecture. This module is specifically 
engineered to categorize maxillary sinus lesions within the de-
tected maxillary sinus images, thereby facilitating accurate di-
agnostic outcomes.
For the inference stage, given an input CT image, the semi-­
supervised maxillary sinus region object detection module au-
tomatically localizes the maxillary sinus ROIs. These detected 
ROIs are then processed by the maxillary sinus lesion classifi-
cation prediction module to obtain probability distributions for 
each ROI.
2.5.1   |   The Maxillary Sinus Area Object 
Detection Module
This module employs Tiny-­YOLOv4 as its network, selected for 
its exceptional performance and real-­time processing capabili-
ties in resource-­constrained environments [38].
The manually annotated dataset was randomly partitioned into 
training, validation, and test sets, following a ratio of 7:2:1, re-
spectively. Subsequently, we amalgamated the training and val-
idation sets of this manually annotated dataset with the output 
generated by the pseudo-­label generation model. This combined 
dataset was then randomly split in an 8:2 ratio to form the defin-
itive training and validation sets for the maxillary sinus detec-
tion model.
To assess the efficacy of the semi-­supervised model, we em-
ployed the test set derived from the manually annotated data-
set as the test set for the maxillary sinus detection model. This 
approach ensures an unbiased evaluation of the model's perfor-
mance on previously unseen data.
2.5.1.1   |   Construction and Training of Object Detection

key components (Figure  2A). The backbone network utilizes

2.5.1.2   |   Semi-­Supervised 
Learning 
Strategy.  This 
study employs a semi-­supervised learning approach based 
on the Teacher-­Student framework to train the Tiny-­YOLOv4 
model, effectively utilizing a substantial volume of unlabeled 
data to mitigate the scarcity of labeled medical image data.
Initially, the Teacher model serves as a pseudo-­label generator, 
predicting outcomes for a large-­scale unlabeled dataset. This pro-
cess automatically generates pseudo-­labels for each unlabeled 
sample, culminating in a pseudo-­labeled dataset. Notably, only 
predictions with a confidence level exceeding 0.7 are retained as 
pseudo-­labels and subsequently utilized as ground truth.
Subsequently, the labeled dataset and pseudo-­labeled dataset are 
amalgamated to construct a new, expansive training set. This 
augmented dataset substantially surpasses the initial annotated 
dataset in scale, providing rich supervisory information for 
training a more generalizable Student model.
The Tiny-­YOLOv4 Student model is then trained on this com-
prehensive dataset. The significant increase in training data 
volume and the enriched supervisory information endow the 
Student model with enhanced feature representation and gen-
eralization capabilities, markedly improving object detection 
performance.
Upon completion of training, the optimized Tiny-­YOLOv4 
Student model is deployed as a maxillary sinus detection model 
to identify ROI, thus accomplishing the semi-­supervised object 
detection task.
2.5.2   |   Classification Module of Maxillary 
Sinus Lesions
To comprehensively evaluate the efficacy of diverse deep 
learning architectures for this task, this study selected four 
representative models encompassing both convolutional neu-
ral networks and vision transformers. The chosen models in-
clude MobileNetV2, ResNet-­50, Swin Transformer, and Vision 
Transformer (ViT). The output ROIs derived from the maxillary 
sinus area object detection module was partitioned into training, 
validation, and test sets, adhering to a ratio of 7:2:1.
2.5.2.1   |   Construction and Training of Classification 
Model.  Two CNN architectures and two Transformer-­based 
networks were employed/utilized in the classification module. 
ResNet-­50 leveraging its exemplary performance in image clas-
sification tasks and its capacity to process complex features [39] 
(Figure 2B). The pivotal innovation of ResNet-­50 lies in its intro-
duction of the residual learning framework, which effectively 
mitigates the gradient vanishing problem in deep networks. 
ResNet-­50 architecture consists of three main parts: an initial 
7 × 7 convolutional and 3 × 3 max pooling layer, followed by 16 
residual blocks arranged in four stages (each block using three 
convolutional layers with shortcuts), and finally a global average 
pooling, fully connected, and Softmax layer for classification.
MobileNetV2, a lightweight convolutional neural network, in-
corporates residual structures and linear bottlenecks [40]. It 
utilizes depth-­wise separable and pointwise convolutions to 
reduce parameters and computational costs while maintaining 
accuracy, making it suitable for resource-­constrained environ-
ments and real-­time applications. ViT applies the Transformer 
architecture to computer vision tasks [41]. It processes images 
by dividing them into fixed-­size patches, embedding these 
patches, and modeling their relationships through self-­attention 
mechanisms. ViT excels in capturing global dependencies, 
demonstrating impressive performance in image classification. 
Swin Transformer, a hierarchical visual Transformer model, 
enhances ViT's performance and efficiency [42]. It introduces 
a local window self-­attention mechanism and employs cross-­
window connections and shifted windows to balance infor-
mation exchange across different scales. This design optimizes 
the trade-­off between accuracy and computational efficiency 
(Figure 2C).
2.5.2.2   |   Model Training.  To enhance model performance 
and expedite the training process, we implemented several 
strategies. Firstly, we employed transfer learning, initializing 
ResNet-­50 with ImageNet pre-­trained weights and freezing 
the convolutional blocks at the first 50 epochs, while fine-­tuning 
only the last convolutional block and the newly appended fully 
connected layer. Secondly, we applied data augmentation tech-
niques to enrich training sample diversity, including random 
cropping, horizontal flipping, rotation, and adjustments to 
brightness, contrast, and saturation.
The training process is performed on a workstation equipped 
with RTX 3090 GPU (24 GB video memory) and implemented 
using the PyTorch 1.8.0 framework. The specific training hyper-
parameter configuration is as follows: the initial learning rate 
is set to 0.0001, the SGD optimizer (momentum = 0.9, weight _ 
decay = 5e−4) is used, the batch size is set to 32, and the total 
number of training rounds is 200 epochs. The cosine learning 
rate scheduling strategy is used. The loss function incorporates 
cross-­entropy loss with label smoothing to mitigate overfitting. 
To address class imbalance, we calculated sample weights for 
each class and applied these class weights to the loss function.
In the deep learning training of dealing with class imbalance, 
we adopt a targeted loss function design and training strategy.

2.5.2.3   |   Visualization of the Classification Module 
of Maxillary Sinus Lesions.  To gain a more profound under-
standing of the performance characteristics of MobileNetV2, 
ResNet50, Swin Transformer, and ViT models in the maxillary 
sinus lesions classification, we employed Gradient-­weighted 
Class Activation Mapping (Grad-­CAM) for interpretability 
analysis. Grad-­CAM is an efficacious model visualization tech-
nique that utilizes gradient information as weights to aggregate 
feature maps, thereby identifying and highlighting the regions 
of focus in the model's decision-­making process [43]. This tech-
nique provides an intuitive visualization of the areas most influ-
ential in generating predictions.
For the MobileNetV2 and ResNet50 architectures, we desig-
nated the final convolutional layer as the target layer for Grad-­
CAM analysis. In contrast, for the Swin Transformer and ViT 
networks, we selected the multilayer perceptron (MLP) layer of 
the penultimate block as the target layer. This study generated 
visual heatmaps for the classification model to elucidate the 
focal points in the model's decision-­making process.

classification performance of the system, four common metrics 
(Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1 score) and the confusion matrix 
of the test dataset were used.

3   |   Results
3.1   |   Maxillary Sinus Object Detection Module
As the number of training iterations increased to 150 epochs, 
both the pseudo-­label generation model and the maxillary sinus 
detection model demonstrated significant convergence in their 
training and validation losses, accompanied by continuous im-
provement in model performance (Figure S3). The PR curves 
of the maxillary sinus area object detection module illustrate 
the performance comparison between the pseudo-­label genera-
tion model and the final maxillary sinus detection model. Both 
models achieved exceptional performance, with mAP values of 
94.33% and 94.03%, respectively. The PR curves maintained high 
precision across a wide range of recall values. The pseudo-­label 
generation model exhibited marginally superior performance, 
although the difference is minimal (Figure 3). Notably, despite 
the incorporation of substantial pseudo-­label data, the model's 
accuracy remained robust. Moreover, this strategy significantly 
enhanced the model's generalization capacity, establishing a 
solid foundation for processing diverse clinical data.
Specifically, the performance metrics for the pseudo-­label gener-
ation model are as follows: AP: 0.9433, Precision: 0.9358, Recall: 
0.8177, F1: 0.8700. The corresponding metrics for the maxillary 
sinus detection model are AP: 0.9403, Precision: 0.9324, Recall: 
0.7945, F1: 0.8600 (Table  1). These quantitative results indi-
cate that both models achieve high-­level detection performance. 
Figure 4 presents a visual comparison of the ROIs annotated by 
different methods. The ROIs delineated by the pseudo-­label gener-
ation model (blue boxes) and the maxillary sinus detection model 
(yellow boxes) exhibit high concordance with the manually an-
notated ROIs by medical professionals (green boxes). This visual 
congruence further corroborates the accuracy and reliability of 
our proposed method in maxillary sinus area localization.

3.2   |   Classification Module of Maxillary Sinus 
Lesions
The classification performance of various algorithms for MSCs. 
These matrices illustrate the comparative efficacy of different 
classification methods in distinguishing between these two 
types of maxillary sinus lesions (Figure 5). Notably, ResNet-­50 
demonstrated superior performance in both coronal and sagittal 
classification diagnostic tasks. We present the loss curves that 
illustrate the model's diagnostic performance on both coronal 
and sagittal planes (Figure S4).
We compared various algorithms for constructing classifica-
tion models, evaluating their performance using metrics such 
as Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1 scores (Tables 2 and 3). 
ResNet-­50 exhibited optimal performance across all metrics. In 
the sagittal plane, ResNet-­50 achieved an impressive Accuracy 
of 0.9836, Precision of 0.9618, Recall of 0.9563, and F1 score of 
0.9590. Similarly, in the coronal plane, the model demonstrated 
robust performance with an Accuracy of 0.9797, Precision of 
0.9485, Recall of 0.9499, and F1 score of 0.9492. These compre-
hensive results underscore ResNet-­50's exceptional capability in 
accurately classifying maxillary sinus lesions across both ana-
tomical planes, outperforming other tested algorithms in this 
specific diagnostic task.
Grad-­CAM effectively identifies and highlights regions of 
interest for various classification algorithm models during 
diagnostic decision-­making. Upon analyzing the heat maps 
generated by different algorithm models in the sagittal and 
coronal planes, we discovered that the ResNet-­50 model exhib-
ited attention patterns remarkably consistent with established 
radiological diagnostic criteria when identifying various 
maxillary sinus lesions. This consistency is evident across 
several types of lesions: Firstly, for pseudocysts, the model 
focused on the acute angle formed between the cyst and the 
sinus wall, as well as the overall cyst morphology. Secondly, 
in cases of mucocele, the model's attention was directed to-
wards the obstruction of the maxillary sinus ostium. Thirdly, 
when assessing mucosal thickening, the model concentrated 
on the area of maximum mucosal thickness at the maxillary 
sinus floor. Lastly, for retention cysts, the model emphasized 
the characteristic near-­right angle formation between the cyst 
and the sinus wall, along with the overall cyst configuration 
(Figures 6 and 7).
These observations demonstrate that the ResNet-­50 model 
has successfully learned to prioritize diagnostically relevant 
features, closely mirroring the approach of experienced radiol-
ogists in maxillary sinus lesion identification and classification.
4   |   Discussion
MSCs represent a significant risk factor in maxillary sinus 
floor elevation procedures. The primary clinical concern asso-
ciated with these cysts is the potential contamination of bone 
graft material and implants in the surgical area due to cyst 
rupture. Moreover, the removal of MSCs presents challenges 
related to excessive mucosal perforation, complicating mu-
cosal repair and potentially necessitating secondary surgical 
intervention.
In clinical practice, practitioners must comprehensively eval-
uate multiple diagnostic indicators, including cyst type, size 
and location, when formulating strategies for maxillary sinus 
floor elevation. The rapid development of AI has made intel-
ligent diagnosis possible, and researchers have attempted to 
develop related models. The maxillary sinus abnormality di-
agnosis model developed by Zeng et al. using target detection 
and classification algorithms, at the optimal threshold, the 
accuracy of the model exceeded 90% [30]. Although the model 
achieved good diagnostic performance, it only performed bi-
nary classification diagnosis for two conditions: normal and 
abnormal maxillary sinuses. Furthermore, the model devel-
oped by Ha et al. using object detection algorithms achieved 
an accuracy rate of 81% for the detection of maxillary sinus 
retention pseudocysts and 90% for the detection of cysts or 
tumors [31]. Altun, Oğuzhan et  al. developed a DL model 
using the YOLOv5x framework for detecting maxillary sinus, 
healthy maxillary sinuses, mucosal thickening, mucous reten-
tion cysts, and sinusitis, with a prediction accuracy of 86% for 
maxillary sinus mucosal cysts [44]. Our study employs a deep 
learning cascade network to predict maxillary sinus mucosal 
lesions, achieving accurate classification of pseudocysts, mu-
coceles, mucosal thickening, and retention cysts. Based on the 
ResNet-­50 architecture, our model demonstrates an accuracy 
of up to 98.36% in diagnosing maxillary sinus lesions in both 
coronal and sagittal plane ROIs. This approach demonstrates 
more refined classification and superior accuracy compared to 
existing methods for similar tasks in the field.
The enhanced performance of our model is primarily attributed 
to the semi-­supervised object detection method utilized in con-
structing a large-­scale maxillary sinus lesion dataset. In con-
trast to previous approaches, we implemented pseudo-­labels 
in conjunction with automated threshold screening, thereby 
maximizing the utilization of unlabeled data. This innovative 
methodology significantly improved the model's generalization 
performance while maintaining high accuracy.
In our model selection for MSC classification, we compared the 
performance of CNNs and Transformers. We evaluated clas-
sic CNN architectures such as ResNet-­50 and MobileNetV2, 
alongside recent Transformer-­based models like ViT and Swin 
Transformer.
Our experimental results on the MSCs classification task demon-
strate that CNN models, such as ResNet-­50 and MobileNetV2,

To enhance the model's interpretability, we employed a visu-
alization technique to elucidate the model's attentional focus 
through the generation of heat maps. Utilizing the GradCAM al-
gorithm, we were able to visually delineate the regions of signif-
icance in the model's decision-­making process. For each model 
architecture, we meticulously selected appropriate target layers 
for heat map generation. These target layers, typically situated 
in the terminal stages of the model, are capable of capturing 
high-­level feature representations.
For the ResNet-­50 architecture, we designated the terminal 
convolutional layer as the target layer for visualization. This 
selection was predicated on the structural characteristics of 
ResNet-­50, as the final convolutional layer is capable of ex-
tracting salient features of cystic formations. Upon visualiza-
tion of the ResNet-­50 heatmap, we observed that the model 
predominantly focused on the angular relationship between the 
pseudocyst wall and the sinus wall, aligning with clinical and 
pathophysiological considerations. In the case of mucocele, we 
noted that the model could localize attention to the sinus ostium 
area in mucocele images. Maxillary sinus mucocele, a mucosal 
cyst resulting from maxillary sinus ostium obstruction, mani-
fests radiologically as complete occlusion of the maxillary sinus 
ostium, edema and obscuration of the ostiomeatal complex, and 
hyperattenuating opacities within the maxillary sinus. These 
findings suggest that ResNet-­50 effectively captures the diag-
nostic hallmarks of MSCs.
For the Swin Transformer and ViT, we selected the MLP layer 
of the penultimate block as the target layer, considering their 
hierarchical structure, attention mechanisms, and capacity for 
global information integration. However, we observed that the 
heatmaps generated from these two models exhibited reduced 
interpretability. This phenomenon may be attributed to several 
factors: Firstly, in contrast to CNNs, which extract features based 
on local receptive fields and spatial localization, ViT segments

the original image. In our study, we noted that the heatmaps of 
Transformer-­based frameworks demonstrated attention across 
the entire image, whereas CNN-­based frameworks exhibited 
more focused areas of attention. Secondly, the multi-­head self-­
attention mechanism in ViT augments the complexity of vi-

the final heatmap.
In the exploration of improving the accuracy of deep learning 
models, the hybrid CNN and Transformer architecture show 
significant potential. With its excellent local feature extraction 
and spatial information processing capabilities, CNN can ef-
fectively capture low-­level features of images; transformer can 
establish long-­range dependencies through the self-­attention 
mechanism, which helps to understand global semantic infor-
mation. The hybrid architecture combining the two not only re-
tains the advantages of CNN ‘s hierarchical feature extraction, 
but also incorporates Transformer ‘s global modeling capabili-
ties. In the future, it may be possible to use CoAtNet to propose a 
new relative attention mechanism that effectively combines the 
advantages of convolution and self-­attention [45]. These hybrid 
architectures can not only improve the expression ability of the 
model, but also alleviate the computational complexity of the 
pure Transformer architecture to a certain extent. By reasonably 
designing the fusion strategies of CNN and Transformer, such 
as the selection of feature levels, the design of attention mecha-
nism, and multi-­scale feature fusion, the accuracy of the model 
can be further improved.

5   |   Conclusion
This study developed a cascaded network framework integrat-
ing object detection and image classification for automatic, 
high-­precision detection and classification of maxillary sinus 
lesions in CBCT images. The innovative application of semi-­
supervised pseudo-­labeling technology effectively reduces data 
annotation costs, providing new insights for related model de-
velopment. Employing the ResNet50 network achieves accurate 
classification of maxillary sinus lesions, offering a powerful aid 
for clinical diagnosis.

Abstract: Objective: Maxillary sinus mucosal cysts represent prevalent oral and maxillofacial diseases, and their precise diagnosis is essential for surgical planning in maxillary sinus floor elevation. This study aimed to develop a deep learning-­based pipeline for the classification of maxillary sinus lesions in cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) images to provide auxiliary support for clinical diagnosis. Methods: This study utilized 45 136 maxillary sinus images from CBCT scans of 541 patients. A cascade network was designed, comprising a semi-­supervised maxillary sinus area object detection module and a maxillary sinus lesions classification module. The object detection module employed a semi-­supervised pseudo-­labelling training strategy to expand the maxillary sinus an- notation dataset. In the classification module, the performance of Convolutional Neural Network and Transformer architectures was compared for maxillary sinus mucosal lesion classification. The object detection and classification modules were evaluated using metrics including Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1 score, and Average Precision, with the object detection module addition- ally assessed using Precision-­Recall Curve. Results: The fully supervised pseudo-­label generation model achieved an average accuracy of 0.9433, while the semi-­supervised maxillary sinus detection model attained 0.9403. ResNet-­50 outperformed in classification, with accuracies of 0.9836 (sagittal) and 0.9797 (coronal). Grad-­CAM visualization confirmed accurate focus on clinically relevant lesion features. Conclusion: The proposed pipeline achieves high-­precision detection and classification of maxillary sinus mucosal lesions, reducing manual annotation while maintaining accuracy.
